name: Wendy Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most days start at the hospital on Carver Street. The agency books me for Hindi and Punjabi, so I might do a cancer clinic at nine, a maternity check at eleven, and then a hearing at the family court after lunch. In the evenings I translate the paper side of it: school letters, birth certificates, tenancy notices, all by hand at my kitchen table.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment a scared grandmother realises someone in the room actually understands her. What wears me out is the agency. They take nearly half of what the hospital pays, they pay me thirty days late, and I'm the one who trains every new interpreter they hire for nothing extra. My partner Tomas drives the number 12 bus, and between us we just about cover the rent on the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, finally some sense. Interpreting isn't a typing job, it's a human job, and I've been saying that at every association meeting for two years. I'd probably post something smug about it, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it doesn't fix anything for me. The agency already cut my document rate from twelve cents a word to nine last spring, and that had nothing to do with AI, it's just them squeezing. I've got about three weeks of rent in the bank, and a plateau doesn't change that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing exactly what I do now, the clinics and the court. I'd push the association again to get a fair minimum rate written into the hospital contract. And I'd try to put fifty a month aside, though I've said that every January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved for a day, then back to the usual knot in my stomach. The worry was never only about machines. It's the late payments and the rent going up again in March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the worry was never only about machines. What's the bill you think about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent, always. Our landlord sent a letter in October about an increase in March, and if the agency pays late that month we'd be borrowing from Tomas's mum again, which I hate. She's lovely about it, but I'm twenty-seven and senior at my job and I still can't cover one bad month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for that, if not the machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The agencies, and the hospitals that hire the cheapest agency because nobody checks quality. A cardiology nurse once told me the agency before ours sent a man who couldn't say 'stent' in Punjabi. Fair rates and proper standards should be a law, not a favour.

say: I'd tell everyone **interpreting is human** work and the hype proved it.
I'd post about it and use it at the next **association meeting**.
think: My real problem is the agency cutting my **document rate** from twelve to nine cents.
With **three weeks of rent** saved, a plateau doesn't make me safe.
do: Keep doing the **hospital clinics** and family court bookings as now.
Push the association for a **minimum rate** in the hospital contract.
Try to save **fifty a month**, starting in January.
feel: Briefly **relieved**, then back to a familiar **knot** about rent and late pay.
S0.quote: I'm twenty-seven and senior at my job and I still can't cover one bad month.
fieldNote: Her worry predates AI: **late payments** from the agency and a **rent rise** in March drive it.
She blames agencies and cheap hospital contracts, and wants **standards in law**.
Pride in her skill sits awkwardly next to borrowing from her **partner's mother**.

steps.text: Keep taking the Hindi and Punjabi clinic bookings at the hospital
Raise a minimum interpreting rate at the next association meeting
Put fifty a month into a separate rent pot from January

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: patients deserve a person, not an app. I'd be loud about it online and I'd want the association to campaign on it. Medical and legal interpreting needs rules about who's allowed to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the document side of my work is gone. Birth certificates and school letters are exactly the sort of writing and checking the card talks about, and that's about a third of my income. The clinics might hold on longer, but the agency will try an app in the outpatient clinics first because it's cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for every campaign the association runs and write to the hospital trust board. I'd cut the gym and the streaming, and Tomas and I would look at a smaller flat. I know people will tell me to learn the AI tools, but I won't put my name on a translation a machine made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, mostly. I'm good at this, I'm one of the people the agency calls when it's hard, and that might not matter at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You won't put your name on a machine translation. What if that's the only document work going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd lose the document work, and I'd be honest about why. A woman last year had her visa delayed because a machine turned 'paternal aunt' into 'mother' on a form. I'd rather earn less than be the person who signs off on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomas the night the agency told you the document work was ending?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tomas (my partner) we need to move somewhere cheaper before the rent rise, not after it. Then I'd probably cry in the bath. He'd say we'll manage, because he always says that, but his bus wages can't carry both of us.

say: I'd insist **patients deserve a person**, not an app.
I'd want the association to campaign for **rules on who interprets**.
think: The **document work**, about a third of my income, is gone in this picture.
The agency will try an **app in outpatients** first because it's cheap.
do: Join every **association campaign** and write to the hospital trust board.
Cut the **gym and streaming** within the first month.
Look at a **smaller flat** with Tomas before the rent rise.
feel: **Frightened**, and hurt that being among the best **might not matter**.
S1.quote: I'd tell Tomas (my partner) we need to move somewhere cheaper before the rent rise, not after it.
fieldNote: She refuses to **post-edit** machine output on principle, even at a cost.
Losing a **third of income** on thin savings is her central fear.
Her answer is **political**: campaigns and letters rather than learning new tools.

steps.text: Write to the hospital trust board about using human interpreters
Join the association's campaign on medical interpreting standards
Cancel the gym and streaming subscriptions this month
Look at cheaper flats with Tomas before the March rent rise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a disaster that governments let happen, and I'd mean it. I'd be on every march. I'd say the people who built these machines owe the rest of us a living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be finished as an interpreter within a year or two. If an AI can do any thinking work as well as a person, it can interpret a cancer diagnosis, and hospitals will take it to save money. Two years isn't enough time for me to become anything else, and I don't have the savings to try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I genuinely don't know. I'd keep taking whatever clinic bookings were left, and I'd lean on Tomas and his family, which I hate. Maybe I'd look at care work, because the robots for hands-on jobs come three years later, but I've never done anything like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Like the floor is going. I don't have a plan, and I don't think I could make one in two years with three weeks of rent saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned care work. What makes you think of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum did care work for twenty years, so I know what it is. It's hands-on, and the robots come later, so maybe it buys three years. But it pays even less than I earn now, and my back is already bad from sitting at the kitchen table translating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about besides yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The patients. Mrs Kaur (a patient I interpret for) has dementia and only trusts me because I've been at every appointment for two years. A machine won't notice when she's confused rather than disagreeing.

say: I'd call it a **disaster** governments allowed to happen.
I'd say the builders **owe us a living** and join the marches.
think: I'd be **finished** as an interpreter within a year or two.
**Two years** is too short to retrain with my savings.
do: Take any **clinic bookings** still offered, for as long as they last.
Lean on **Tomas's family** for help with rent.
Think about **care work**, since robots arrive three years later.
feel: **Sick**, as if the floor is going, with **no plan** at all.
S2.quote: Two years isn't enough time for me to become anything else, and I don't have the savings to try.
fieldNote: With **no plan** and almost no savings, she is overwhelmed rather than angry.
She sees **care work** as a three-year bridge, not a future.
Her strongest concern is for vulnerable **patients** like Mrs Kaur.

steps.text: Keep taking whatever hospital clinic bookings the agency still offers
Ask Tomas's family to help cover rent for a while
Join marches demanding public support for displaced workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the fast one, but I'd have more time to organise. I'd say we need a plan for people like me now, while there are five years. I'd push for public money for retraining and a guaranteed income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means the document work goes first, then the interpreting, probably by 2030. I'd have a few years of shrinking income rather than a cliff. It's still the end of the job I trained six years for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first two years to get a care or community support qualification at the college on Mill Road, in the evenings, if it was free. I'd keep interpreting during the day. Tomas and I would put off any idea of a bigger place and save whatever we could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Less panic than two years, but I'd be watching my own job drain away slowly, which might be worse in its own way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'if it was free'. What happens if the course costs money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I wouldn't do it, honestly. I can't take on a loan with three weeks of savings and an agency that pays late. That's why I keep saying the government should pay for this, not individual people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything about interpreting still be worth holding on to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the court work, if the law insisted on a human interpreter for a while. Judges are slow to change, which for once might help. I'd hold on to the family court bookings as long as they lasted.

say: I'd say we need a **plan now** while there are five years.
I'd push for **public money** for retraining and a guaranteed income.
think: Documents go first, then **interpreting by 2030**, so income shrinks gradually.
It's still the end of the job I **trained six years** for.
do: Study for a **care qualification** in the evenings, but only if it's free.
Keep the **family court bookings** as long as judges insist on humans.
Delay any **bigger place** and save what we can.
feel: **Heavy**, watching the job **drain away** slowly rather than all at once.
S3.quote: I can't take on a loan with three weeks of savings and an agency that pays late.
fieldNote: Extra time helps her only if **retraining is free**; she won't borrow.
She sees **court rules** as the last protection for human interpreters.
She still expects to **lose her job**, just more slowly.

steps.text: Enrol in a free evening care qualification at the Mill Road college
Keep the family court interpreting bookings for as long as offered
Lobby the local councillor for free retraining and income support
Put off moving to a bigger flat and save the difference

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so there's no excuse for leaving people behind. I'd want unions and the association planning it with the government, not tech firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is different for me. I'd be thirty-seven when it arrives, which is young enough to start something else. I'd still lose interpreting in the end, but I wouldn't be pushed off a cliff at twenty-nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep interpreting for maybe five or six more years while training part-time as a mental health support worker. That's people work, and it's hands-on enough that the robots are three years further off. I'd also try to keep fifty a month going so I'm not starting the change with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can breathe. There's a version of this where I come out all right, which I couldn't say about the other two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why mental health support, rather than something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've sat in so many appointments where the medical part took ten minutes and the fear took an hour. I'm already doing half that job without the title. I'd rather get paid for the half that matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change about how you work now, today, knowing a decade was coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still not use the AI tools, if that's what you're asking. But I'd stop doing the free training for the agency's new interpreters and charge for it. If my time is running out, I want it paid for.

say: I'd say **ten years** leaves no excuse for leaving people behind.
I'd want **unions and the association** planning it with government.
think: At **thirty-seven** I'd still be young enough to start something else.
I'd lose interpreting eventually, but not **at twenty-nine**.
do: Keep interpreting for **five or six years** while training part-time.
Train as a **mental health support** worker.
Start **charging the agency** for training new interpreters.
feel: **Worried** but able to breathe, seeing a way to come out **all right**.
S4.quote: I've sat in so many appointments where the medical part took ten minutes and the fear took an hour.
fieldNote: A decade turns panic into a **career plan** built on her emotional skills.
She still refuses **AI tools**, but starts valuing her time differently.
The planned move into **mental health support** grows from what she already does.

steps.text: Train part-time as a mental health support worker
Keep interpreting at the hospital and court for five or six years
Charge the agency a fee for training new interpreters

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question, because there's no time and no money to do anything. What would help is free retraining that pays you while you study, and rules that say a sick person gets a human interpreter. That's not charity, it's basic safety.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who's already been hurt. Some of the interpreters I trained have left for supermarket jobs because the agency rates were so bad. The machines aren't the first thing to push us out, they're just the latest.

headlineQuote: The machines aren't the first thing to push us out, they're just the latest.
portrait: Wendy is a **27-year-old** Hindi and Punjabi interpreter who trains her agency's new starters for free.
She refuses to use **AI tools** and won't sign off on a machine translation.
Her savings cover **three weeks of rent**, and her partner Tomas drives a bus.
She moves from anxious in AI Plateau to **panicked** in AGI by 2028, then steadies with ten years.
She blames **agencies and governments**, and answers through campaigns and the translators' association.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time and no money to change course.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** and a legal right to a **human interpreter** for patients.
